'''Nabil Mishreky Lawandy''' (born March 12, 1957) is an American [[physicist]], [[inventor]], academic, and businessman. After 18 years as a professor of Engineering and Physics at [[Brown University]], Lawandy founded [[Spectra Systems Corporation]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.spsy.com/about-us/executive-team/|title=Executive Team {{!}} World Leader In Security Technology|website=Spectra Systems|access-date=2019-11-18}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.marketscreener.com/business-leaders/Nabil-Lawandy-06LDST-E/biography/?iCStream=0|title=Nabil M. Lawandy - Biography|last=MarketScreener|website=www.marketscreener.com|access-date=2019-11-18}}</ref> He is currently the President, and Chief Executive Officer of Spectra Systems Corporation, a [[London Stock Exchange]]-listed company<ref name=":0" /> and is currently a Professor of Research at Brown University in the School of Engineering. Technology invented by Lawandy is used by many of the world's central banks to protect against [[counterfeit]]ing of banknotes.

== Early life ==
Lawandy was born in [[Cairo, Egypt]] to Mishreky Aziz Lawandy and Anastasia Sakelaridis. At the age of eight, the Lawandy family immigrated to Canada and then to the United States, where they became naturalized citizens. Lawandy grew up in northern Virginia and enrolled at the [[Johns Hopkins University]] where he graduated with Honors in 1977 and proceeded to complete his Master's from the same university in 1979. The very next year, he completed his [[Ph.D.]] in [[chemical physics]] at the age of 23.<ref name=":1" />

== Career ==
'''Work at NASA'''

Working at the [[NASA]] [[Goddard Space Flight Center]], Lawandy was part of a team that developed optically pumped [[far-infrared]] molecular [[laser]]s for use as [[local oscillator]]s in astronomical [[heterodyne]] detection systems. The lasers developed were used to map the concentration of [[carbon monoxide]] (CO) in the [[Orion Nebula]] using the [[Keck telescope]]s at [[Mauna Kea]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/search.jsp?R=19840046473|title=NTRS|date=January 1982|website=|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|last1=Buhl |first1=D. |last2=Chin |first2=G. |last3=Fetterman |first3=H. R. |last4=Koepf |first4=G. A. |last5=Peck |first5=D. D. }}</ref>

While still at NASA, Lawandy was one of the first to observe [[self-pulsing instabilities]] and [[deterministic chaos]] related to the [[Lorenz instability]] and [[dynamic Stark effect]]s in optically pumped molecular lasers.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lawandy|first1=N.|last2=Koepf|first2=G.|date=July 1980|title=Relaxation oscillations in optically pumped molecular lasers|journal=IEEE Journal of Quantum Electronics|volume=16|issue=7|pages=701–703|doi=10.1109/JQE.1980.1070560|bibcode=1980IJQE...16..701L }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lawandy|first1=Nabil M.|last2=Koepf|first2=Gerhard A.|date=1982-01-01|title=Determination of vibrational matrix elements using heterodyne measurements of two-photon splittings in optically pumped molecular lasers|journal=Physical Review A|volume=25|issue=1|pages=433–436|doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.25.433|bibcode=1982PhRvA..25..433L }}</ref>

'''Work at Brown University'''

After joining the faculty at Brown University in 1981, Lawandy's work throughout his academic career was a combination of experiment and theory. His early work focused on instabilities and chaos in single and [[multimode laser]]s with particular emphasis in coherently driven instabilities associated with three-level systems.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ryan|first1=J.|last2=Lawandy|first2=N.|date=November 1986|title=Density matrix solutions for the susceptibilities of a three-level system with arbitrary relaxation rates and field strengths|journal=IEEE Journal of Quantum Electronics|volume=22|issue=11|pages=2075–2078|doi=10.1109/JQE.1986.1072911|bibcode=1986IJQE...22.2075R }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/search.jsp?R=19820052834|title=Lawandy, N. Lawandy has served as a thesis advisor to 19 Ph.D. students during his tenure as a Professor at Brown University and delivered over forty invited lectures on various research topics. His research has resulted in over 180 papers in refereed journals and 119 conference presentations and has been cited over 3200 times.

Lawandy's career has been covered in many scientific journals and magazines as well as television segments, including [[The Economist]], [[Scientific American]], [[Science News]], [[Wall Street Journal]], [[Los Angeles Times]], [[Boston Globe]], [[Fox News]], and BBC.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/1998/05/14/colourful-visions|title=Colourful visions|date=1998-05-14|newspaper=The Economist|access-date=2019-11-18|issn=0013-0613}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-xpm-2014-jan-08-la-sci-sn-scientists-launder-dirty-money-20140108-story.html|title=Scientists experiment with money laundering|date=2014-01-08|website=Los Angeles Times|access-date=2019-11-18}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/paulrodgers/2014/01/31/its-called-filthy-lucre-for-a-reason/|title=The Problem With Dirty Money|last=Rodgers|first=Paul|website=Forbes|access-date=2019-11-18}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2014/01/18/the-benefits-of-money-laundering|title=The benefits of money laundering|date=2014-01-18|newspaper=The Economist|access-date=2019-11-18|issn=0013-0613}}</ref>

== Patents and awards ==
Lawandy holds over 100 published US and international patents in a number of applications spanning optical materials, processes, and devices and authentication technology.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://patents.justia.com/inventor/nabil-lawandy|title=Nabil Lawandy Inventions, Patents and Patent Applications - Justia Patents Search|website=patents.justia.com|access-date=2019-11-18}}</ref> He is an [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation|Alfred P. Sloan]] Fellow, a recipient of a [[Cottrell Award]], the [[Presidential Young Investigator Award]], a 1995 [[Photonics Circle of Excellence Award]], the [[Slater Foundation Innovation Award]], and the [[Rolex Awards for Enterprise|Rolex Prize]] for his work on using Random Lasers for Photo-medicine.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sloan.org/|title=Home|website=sloan.org|access-date=2019-11-18}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://rctech.com/about-us/foundation/|title=Frederick Gardner Cottrell Foundation|website=Research Corporation Technologies|access-date=2019-11-18}}</ref>

He has served as an editor for [[Optics Communications]] and [[Current Topics in Optics]] as well as on the scientific advisory boards of [[Orchid BioComputer]] and [[Finesse Solutions]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20170214006523/en/Thermo-Fisher-Scientific-Completes-Acquisition-Finesse-Solutions|title=Thermo Fisher Scientific Completes Acquisition of Finesse Solutions, Inc.|date=2017-02-14|website=www.businesswire.com|access-date=2019-11-18}}</ref>
